Reading recap, Q&A and polling questions¶

One step at a time, then from the Euler loop to solve_ivp(): derivs, sol.t and sol.y, t_eval, events

Solving an ODE step by step¶

The ball from Preclass 11: $\dfrac{dh}{dt} = v$, $\dfrac{dv}{dt} = -g$, start $h(0) = h_0 = 0$, $v(0) = v_0 = 10$ m/s. So state = [h, v], state0 = [h0, v0]

The same three steps in code¶

derivs gives the slopes, the step multiplies them by dt, the new state replaces the old one

In [ ]:
def derivs(t, state):
    h, v = state
    return [v, -9.81]                   # [dh/dt, dv/dt]

dt = 0.5
t, state = 0, [0, 10]                   # state0 = [h0, v0]
for step in range(3):
    dhdt, dvdt = derivs(t, state)       # the slopes at the old state
    h, v = state
    state = [h + dhdt * dt, v + dvdt * dt]   # new state replaces old
    t = t + dt
    print(t, [round(x, 1) for x in state])

Reading recap: from the Euler loop to solve_ivp()¶

Ingredient Euler loop (11.1 names) solve_ivp() (11.2)
the physics the update lines h + t_step * v, v + t_step * a derivs(t, state) returns [dh/dt, dv/dt] = [v, -g]
the time span t_start, t_end t_span = (0, 2)
the initial conditions h_start, v_start (= h0, v0) state0 = [h0, v0]
the step size t_step (= dt): you choose it, fixed the solver chooses; cap it with max_step=dt 
sol = solve_ivp(derivs, t_span, state0)    # derivs without ( )
  • The loop is gone: solve_ivp() does the stepping. Your job: the physics in derivs
  • From here on: state, state0, derivs, dt, t_span (the Euler column keeps the Preclass 11.1 names)

derivs(t, state): what goes in, what comes out¶

def derivs(t, state):
    h, v = state            # in: the time, then the current state
    return [v, -9.81]       # out: [dh/dt, dv/dt]
  • In: always t first, then state, even if t is not used
  • Out: the derivatives of the state (the slopes of the step triangles), in the same order as the state. Not the new state: there is no dt in derivs
  • solve_ivp() calls derivs many times, at times it chooses

Reading the solution: sol.t and sol.y¶

sol = solve_ivp(derivs, t_span, state0)
  • sol.t: 1D array of the times
  • sol.y: 2D array, rows = state variables, columns = times
  • sol.y[0]: all the heights. sol.y[1]: all the velocities
  • sol.y[:, 0]: the state at the first time, state0 = [h0, v0]. sol.y[0, -1]: the height at the last time

Which times come back: t_eval vs the solver's steps¶

  • No t_eval: sol.t holds the solver's own steps: uneven, and you do not choose them
  • max_step=dt only caps the solver's step size: more steps, still the solver's times
  • t_eval=times: sol.t is exactly your array (inside t_span). The solver still steps on its own inside
  • Either way sol.y has one column per time in sol.t

Events: terminal and direction¶

def hit_ground(t, state):
    return state[0]            # an event when this crosses 0
hit_ground.terminal = True     # stop the solver there
hit_ground.direction = -1      # only from + to -

sol = solve_ivp(derivs, (0, 5), state0, events=[hit_ground])
  • Return a value that is 0 at the event: "at 4 m" → state[0] - 4
  • terminal: True stops; False (default) only records the time
  • direction: -1 from + to −, +1 from − to +, 0 (default) both
  • Set the attributes after the def, not inside it

Events and t_eval together¶

  • A terminal event stops the solver early, so sol.t stops early too
  • With t_eval: sol.t holds only your times before the stop
  • The event time is not added to sol.t. It is in sol.t_events[0]

Poll Q1: The state is [h, v]. What does this print?

In [ ]:
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

def derivs(t, state):
    h, v = state
    return [-9.81, v]

sol = solve_ivp(derivs, [0, 1], [0, 0], t_eval=[0, 1])
print(np.round(sol.y[:, -1], 2))

A) [-4.91 -9.81]
B) [-9.81 0. ]
C) [ 0. -9.81]
D) Error: the order does not matter

Poll Q2: What does this print?

In [ ]:
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

def derivs(t, state):
    h, v = state
    return [v, -9.81]

sol = solve_ivp(derivs, [0, 2], [0, 10], t_eval=np.linspace(0, 2, 5))
print(np.round(sol.y[1], 2))

A) [0. 3.77 5.1 3.96 0.38]
B) [10. 5.1 0.19 -4.72 -9.62]
C) [3.77 5.1 ]
D) [ 0. 10.]

Poll Q3: What does this print?

In [ ]:
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

def derivs(t, state):
    h, v = state
    return [v, -9.81]

sol = solve_ivp(derivs, [0, 2], [0, 10], max_step=0.01,
                t_eval=np.linspace(0, 2, 5))
print(len(sol.t), sol.y.shape)

A) 5 (2, 5)
B) 201 (2, 201)
C) 5 (2, 201)
D) 5 (5, 2)

Poll Q4: A ball is thrown up at 10 m/s from the ground. What does this print?

In [ ]:
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

def derivs(t, state):
    h, v = state
    return [v, -9.81]

def at_4m(t, state):
    return state[0] - 4
at_4m.terminal = True
at_4m.direction = 1

sol = solve_ivp(derivs, [0, 3], [0, 10], events=[at_4m])
print(np.round(sol.t_events[0], 2), round(sol.t[-1], 2))

A) [0.55] 0.55
B) [1.49] 1.49
C) [0.55] 3.0
D) [0.55 1.49] 3.0

Events and t_eval together: thrown up at 5 m/s from 1 m high¶

def hit_ground(t, state):
    return state[0]
hit_ground.terminal = True
hit_ground.direction = -1

sol = solve_ivp(derivs, [0, 3], [1, 5], t_eval=np.linspace(0, 3, 7),
                events=[hit_ground])
print(sol.t)              # [0.  0.5 1. ]
print(sol.t_events[0])    # [1.19]
  • The ball lands at $t = 1.19$ s and the solver stops: sol.t keeps only the t_eval times before that
  • The event time is in sol.t_events[0], not in sol.t

Tools compute, YOU verify¶

  • Euler with a big dt drifts away from the true answer (step by step, dt = 0.5: 7.6 m instead of 4.0 m): you will measure it in Homework 12
  • solve_ivp() chooses its own steps and controls the error. It can still give a smooth, wrong answer: a derivs in the wrong order (Poll Q1) runs without an error
  • So check every solution: a known case ($h_{max} = v_0^2 / 2g$), conservation of energy, limits, units
